prompt: What best describes Microsoft Defender for Cloud (MDC)?
choices: A CNAPP combining posture management with workload protection
An identity governance tool for just-in-time role activation and review
A network firewall service for inspecting east-west traffic
A SIEM that only stores and queries security log data
correctAnswers: A CNAPP combining posture management with workload protection
explanation: Defender for Cloud is both halves at once: posture management asks whether you are configured safely, workload protection asks whether you are under attack. The SIEM option is the tempting neighbour and describes Microsoft Sentinel, whereas Defender for Cloud produces the alerts a SIEM would then correlate rather than storing and querying logs itself.

prompt: Four security questions, four capabilities. Assign the one that answers each; two capabilities in the list answer none of them.

targets.label: Are we configured safely? — one impact-weighted percentage across the estate
Are we being attacked right now? — runtime alerts for a given resource type
Which internet-facing assets do we own, including ones nobody remembers?
Which known CVEs exist on our machines and container images?

explanation: The first two are the CSPM and CWP halves of the product and the split is worth internalizing: posture is a configuration question answered continuously, workload protection is an attack question answered in real time. The other two narrow further — EASM looks inward from outside, MDVM looks at software versions. Neither unused capability is a discovery tool: the compliance dashboard maps posture to a standard, and automation rules act on incidents that already exist.

prompt: Which question does CWP (workload protection) answer?
choices: Are we being attacked right now?
Are we configured safely across the estate today?
What does our Secure Score currently show?
Which standards are we compliant with?
correctAnswers: Are we being attacked right now?
explanation: Workload protection is the runtime half and produces alerts as events happen. The configuration question is CSPM, and Secure Score is how CSPM reports itself, whereas neither says anything about an attack in progress — two of the distractors are therefore the same half of the product asked in two ways.

prompt: Which environments can Microsoft Defender for Cloud govern?
choices: Azure, AWS, GCP, and on-premises resources connected via Arc
Any cloud, but only if Microsoft Sentinel is also deployed there
Azure and AWS only, since GCP is not supported at all
Azure subscriptions only, and nothing outside them
correctAnswers: Azure, AWS, GCP, and on-premises resources connected via Arc
explanation: Multicloud is native: AWS and GCP connect through their own identity federation, and anything else arrives via Arc. The Sentinel-dependency option is the tempting one because the two products are usually discussed together, whereas they are independent — Defender for Cloud governs posture with or without a SIEM.

prompt: What is the Secure Score in Microsoft Defender for Cloud?
choices: A percentage summarizing how many weighted recommendations pass
The number of Defender plans currently enabled on the subscription
A count of the security incidents currently open in Sentinel
A per-resource severity rating for each discovered CVE
correctAnswers: A percentage summarizing how many weighted recommendations pass
explanation: Secure Score aggregates recommendations weighted by impact, so it measures configuration rather than activity. Counting enabled Defender plans is the tempting proxy and measures spend instead of posture — a subscription can have every plan on and a poor score, which is exactly the confusion the score exists to prevent.

prompt: Recommendations in Defender for Cloud are grouped into security controls. When does a control contribute its points to the Secure Score?
choices: Only when every resource covered by that control is healthy
Only after a Defender plan is purchased for that control area
Automatically after 30 days, whatever the resource state
As soon as any single resource in the control is healthy
correctAnswers: Only when every resource covered by that control is healthy
explanation: A control is all-or-nothing, which is why fixing nine of ten resources moves the score not at all and finishing the tenth moves it in one step. Expecting partial credit is the tempting model and it makes remediation look ineffective — the practical consequence is to finish a control rather than to spread effort across several.

prompt: What is the most effective way to raise Secure Score quickly?
choices: Remediate the highest-impact recommendations first
Remediate the recommendations in alphabetical order
Enable every paid Defender plan immediately
Remove low-scoring resources from the inventory
correctAnswers: Remediate the highest-impact recommendations first
explanation: Recommendations are impact-weighted, so the order in which you work through them changes how fast the score moves. Enabling every paid plan is the tempting shortcut because it feels like buying security, whereas plans add detection rather than satisfying recommendations and the score barely responds.

prompt: What does the free, foundational CSPM tier include by default for every Azure subscription?
choices: Secure Score, asset inventory, and MCSB recommendations
External Attack Surface Management insights and discovery
Agentless malware scanning of the virtual machine disks
Attack path analysis and the cloud security explorer
correctAnswers: Secure Score, asset inventory, and MCSB recommendations
explanation: The free tier gives you the score, the inventory and the benchmark recommendations, which is enough to know where you stand without buying anything. Attack path analysis and the cloud security explorer are the tempting additions and are exactly what the paid Defender CSPM plan adds — the line between the two tiers is the most-tested fact in this objective.

prompt: A subscription has never enabled any paid Defender plan. Which capability is still available?
choices: Secure Score and the baseline MCSB recommendations
Agentless vulnerability and malware scanning of disks
Attack path analysis across the estate
Cloud security explorer graph queries
correctAnswers: Secure Score and the baseline MCSB recommendations
explanation: Foundational CSPM is on by default and costs nothing, so the score and the benchmark recommendations are always there. Agentless scanning is the tempting answer because it needs no agent and therefore feels free, whereas "no agent" is about deployment rather than licensing — it requires a paid plan.

prompt: Which of the following is added specifically by the paid Defender CSPM plan, not the free tier?
choices: The cloud security explorer
MCSB baseline recommendations
The asset inventory view
Secure Score percentage
correctAnswers: The cloud security explorer
explanation: The explorer runs graph queries over the security graph, and that graph is what the paid plan builds. The MCSB recommendations are the tempting answer because the benchmark sounds like a premium feature, whereas it is the default standard every subscription is scored against for free.

prompt: What does attack path analysis in Defender CSPM provide?
choices: A visualization of exploitable chains from exposure to sensitive assets
A pass or fail compliance report against the ISO 27001 standard controls
A list of the missing patches on one individual virtual machine
A record of AWS IAM role trust relationships, and nothing else
correctAnswers: A visualization of exploitable chains from exposure to sensitive assets
explanation: The value is the chain rather than the individual finding: an exposed VM plus a vulnerability plus a path to sensitive data is a different priority from any of the three alone. The single-VM patch list is the tempting answer and is what MDVM produces, whereas it says nothing about what that VM can reach.

prompt: What is the cloud security explorer used for?
choices: Running graph queries over your posture to find risk combinations
Managing the automation rules and the playbooks in Microsoft Sentinel
Editing the Azure Policy definitions assigned in a subscription
Rotating the keys held in Key Vault automatically
correctAnswers: Running graph queries over your posture to find risk combinations
explanation: The explorer is the query interface to the same graph attack path analysis draws on, which is what lets you ask for a combination nobody wrote a recommendation for. Editing Policy definitions is the tempting neighbour because both concern configuration, whereas Policy changes what is enforced and the explorer only asks questions.

prompt: A security team wants to find 'internet-exposed VMs with a known vulnerability that can reach a database containing sensitive data.' Which capability and tier delivers this?
choices: Attack path analysis or cloud security explorer, in Defender CSPM
The asset inventory, which is available in the free foundational tier
The regulatory compliance dashboard, available in the free tier
Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management on its own
correctAnswers: Attack path analysis or cloud security explorer, in Defender CSPM
explanation: The question joins three facts about three different resources, which only a graph can answer — and the graph comes with the paid plan. MDVM alone is the tempting answer because it supplies the vulnerability half, whereas it cannot express exposure or reachability, so it would return every vulnerable VM rather than the few that matter.

prompt: What is the Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark (MCSB)?
choices: The built-in default standard your environment is scored against
A pack of analytics rule templates for Microsoft Sentinel content
A paid add-on standard that must be purchased separately
A replacement for the ISO 27001 and PCI-DSS assessments
correctAnswers: The built-in default standard your environment is scored against
explanation: MCSB is assigned by default and is what Secure Score reflects before you add any other standard. Reading it as a replacement for ISO 27001 or PCI-DSS is the misconception that matters commercially: those are added alongside it in the regulatory compliance dashboard, whereas MCSB never satisfies an external auditor on its own.

prompt: What does the regulatory compliance dashboard in Defender for Cloud do?
choices: Maps your estate against formal standards, with per-control evidence
Calculates the Security Compute Unit consumption of Microsoft Security Copilot
Lists every CVE affecting the container images in your registries
Shows the trust relationship between your tenant and AWS accounts
correctAnswers: Maps your estate against formal standards, with per-control evidence
explanation: Each control shows pass or fail with the resources behind the verdict, which is what makes it usable as audit evidence rather than as a dashboard. The CVE list is the tempting answer because it is also a compliance concern, whereas vulnerabilities are MDVM findings and appear nowhere in a control-by-control assessment.

prompt: Complete the statement describing how a new compliance standard such as PCI-DSS v4 is added and scoped.
template: A standard is added under [[b1]], and it can be assigned at [[b2]].

options: Defender for Cloud ▸ Regulatory compliance ▸ Manage compliance policies
Microsoft Entra admin center ▸ Identity Governance
blanks.correctValue: Defender for Cloud ▸ Regulatory compliance ▸ Manage compliance policies

options: a management group or a subscription
the tenant root only, with no narrower scope
blanks.correctValue: a management group or a subscription

explanation: The scope is the half people get wrong: a standard is assigned at a management group or a subscription, never at a resource group or a single resource — so an estate that needs PCI-DSS on part of itself is organized by subscription rather than by resource group. The Sentinel Content hub is the tempting path because that is where analytics content is added, whereas compliance standards live in Defender for Cloud.

prompt: At what scope can a regulatory compliance standard be assigned in Defender for Cloud?
choices: A management group or a subscription
The tenant root only, with no narrower scope
An individual resource, and nothing wider
A resource group, and nothing wider
correctAnswers: A management group or a subscription
explanation: Assignment happens at a management group or a subscription, which is why compliance boundaries have to line up with subscription structure. The resource-group option is the tempting one because that is the usual unit of Azure governance, whereas compliance standards deliberately sit above it.

prompt: Why does the regulatory compliance dashboard double as audit preparation?
choices: Each control shows pass or fail with evidence an auditor can use
It disables non-compliant resources until they have been corrected
It automatically generates a signed compliance certificate
It reports only on Azure, so a multicloud audit is out of scope
correctAnswers: Each control shows pass or fail with evidence an auditor can use
explanation: The dashboard produces per-control evidence, which is the artefact an audit actually asks for. The signed-certificate option is the tempting overreach: Defender for Cloud reports your state and never attests to it, so certification still comes from an auditor rather than from the portal.

prompt: What is a Defender workload protection ('Defender for X') plan?
choices: A per-resource-type threat-protection plan that adds runtime alerts
A free posture recommendation set applied to every subscription in scope
A Conditional Access policy scoped to one Azure resource type
A KQL query saved in the Microsoft Sentinel Content hub
correctAnswers: A per-resource-type threat-protection plan that adds runtime alerts
explanation: Each plan is bought and toggled per resource type, and what it adds is detection at runtime. The free posture recommendation set is the tempting confusion with foundational CSPM, whereas that is the always-on configuration half — enabling a Defender plan changes what you are told about attacks rather than about misconfiguration.

prompt: Where do you turn on a specific Defender plan, such as Defender for Storage, for a subscription?
choices: Defender for Cloud ▸ Environment settings ▸ Defender plans
Microsoft Sentinel ▸ Automation ▸ Create a new automation rule
Microsoft Entra admin center ▸ Roles and administrators
Azure Policy ▸ Assignments ▸ Assign initiative
correctAnswers: Defender for Cloud ▸ Environment settings ▸ Defender plans
explanation: Every plan is enabled per environment under Environment settings, which is worth memorising because the path is identical for Storage, Servers, Containers and AI Services. Azure Policy is the tempting alternative since Defender plans can be enforced by policy, whereas the policy assigns the setting rather than being where the toggle lives.

prompt: A team enables Defender for Servers on a subscription. What happens to Defender for Storage on the same subscription?
choices: It remains off — each plan is a separate, independently billed toggle
Defender for Servers cannot be enabled unless Defender for Storage is too
It is enabled automatically, but billed separately from Servers
It is enabled automatically, at no additional cost at all
correctAnswers: It remains off — each plan is a separate, independently billed toggle
explanation: Plans are independent, so enabling one leaves every other exactly as it was — which is how estates end up with storage accounts nobody is watching. Believing the plans imply one another is the assumption to remove, and neither dependency exists: Servers does not require Storage, and Storage is not switched on for free alongside it.

prompt: What is a common sub-option configured within a plan's settings, e.g. for Defender for Servers?
choices: Choosing between Plan 1 and Plan 2 tiers
Choosing which regulatory standard applies
Choosing which Sentinel workspace to use
Choosing the Secure Score weighting formula
correctAnswers: Choosing between Plan 1 and Plan 2 tiers
explanation: Defender for Servers exposes its Plan 1 and Plan 2 tiers as a sub-option inside the plan settings, which is where the choice between EDR-only and the full posture feature set is made. The Sentinel workspace option is the tempting neighbour because Defender data does flow to a workspace, whereas that binding is configured in Sentinel rather than in a Defender plan.

prompt: How does Defender for Cloud authenticate to a connected AWS account to read configuration and deploy protections?
choices: Through AWS identity federation, assuming an IAM role — no stored keys
By storing a permanent AWS access key and secret in the Azure connector
By requiring the AWS root account password to be supplied
By requiring a VPN tunnel between the AWS VPC and Azure
correctAnswers: Through AWS identity federation, assuming an IAM role — no stored keys
explanation: Federation means Defender for Cloud assumes a role you created, so no long-lived credential is stored anywhere. The permanent access key is the tempting mental model because that is how most third-party AWS integrations used to work, whereas it is exactly the pattern the connector was designed to avoid.

prompt: Build the sequence that connects an AWS account to Defender for Cloud. Not every action in the pool belongs in the answer.
poolItems: Add an AWS environment in Defender for Cloud, giving a connector name and the AWS account ID
Run the template in the AWS account so it creates the IAM role Defender assumes
Confirm AWS recommendations and Secure Score data appear in Defender for Cloud
Paste a permanent AWS access key and secret into the connector
Launch an EC2 instance running the Log Analytics agent
Establish a VPN tunnel between the AWS VPC and an Azure virtual network
correctOrder: Add an AWS environment in Defender for Cloud, giving a connector name and the AWS account ID
Run the template in the AWS account so it creates the IAM role Defender assumes
Confirm AWS recommendations and Secure Score data appear in Defender for Cloud
explanation: The template is generated for the connector you just created, so the connector comes first and the role it references cannot exist before it. The three excluded actions are each a different wrong model of how this works: a stored access key is what federation replaces, no compute is deployed in the AWS account, and nothing here needs network connectivity at all — the connector reads the AWS control plane over its API.

prompt: Which information is required when adding an AWS environment in Defender for Cloud, before running the CloudFormation template?
choices: A connector name and the AWS account ID, single or Organization
The AWS root account password and its MFA device serial number, both
A virtual network peering configuration between AWS and Azure
A Microsoft Sentinel workspace resource ID for the connector
correctAnswers: A connector name and the AWS account ID, single or Organization
explanation: Only a name and the account ID are needed, and choosing the Organization management account is what makes the connector cover every member account. Asking for the root password is the tempting assumption from the old integration model, whereas federation means Defender never holds an AWS credential at all.

prompt: How is connecting a GCP project to Defender for Cloud similar to connecting AWS?
choices: It also uses native identity federation, run via a script rather than a template
It requires a GCP service account key to be stored permanently in the Azure connector
GCP cannot be connected at all — only AWS and Azure are supported
It requires the same CloudFormation template that AWS uses
correctAnswers: It also uses native identity federation, run via a script rather than a template
explanation: The principle is identical and only the mechanics differ: GCP federation is established by a script run in Cloud Shell or Terraform instead of a CloudFormation template, which is AWS-specific. The stored service-account key is the tempting answer and is precisely what federation exists to avoid on both clouds.

prompt: What does Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management (MDVM) find?
choices: Missing patches and vulnerable software on machines and images
Internet-facing domains and IP addresses that the organization owns
Azure Policy assignments that are misconfigured or unassigned
Microsoft Sentinel incidents that have no assigned owner yet
correctAnswers: Missing patches and vulnerable software on machines and images
explanation: MDVM answers a software-version question: which known CVEs are present on machines and container images. Internet-facing domains and addresses are the closest miss and are what EASM discovers — one looks at what your assets are running, the other at which assets exist and are reachable.

prompt: What does External Attack Surface Management (EASM) find?
choices: Internet-facing domains, IPs, certificates and services you own
Missing operating-system patches on the internal virtual machines
Azure resources that are non-compliant with an assigned policy
Known CVEs inside the base images used by your containers
correctAnswers: Internet-facing domains, IPs, certificates and services you own
explanation: EASM looks at your organization the way an outsider would, which is why it surfaces forgotten shadow IT that no inventory of your subscriptions contains. The patch and CVE options are tempting because both are vulnerability work, whereas they describe MDVM and presuppose you already know the asset exists.

prompt: For each statement about the free foundational tier and the paid Defender CSPM plan, select Yes if it is true.

statements.text: Secure Score is only available once Defender CSPM has been purchased.
Attack path analysis requires the paid Defender CSPM plan.
The cloud security explorer is part of the free foundational tier.
Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark recommendations are included at no cost.

explanation: The line runs between reporting and reasoning: Secure Score, the asset inventory and the MCSB recommendations are free, whereas attack path analysis and the cloud security explorer both depend on the security graph the paid plan builds. Assuming the score is behind the paywall is the more expensive error of the two, since it leads teams to buy a plan for a capability they already had.

prompt: Which two statements correctly describe the free foundational CSPM tier? (Choose two.)
choices: It is active by default for every Azure subscription
It includes Secure Score and MCSB recommendations
It includes agentless disk scanning of virtual machines
It includes External Attack Surface Management insights
correctAnswers: It is active by default for every Azure subscription
It includes Secure Score and MCSB recommendations
explanation: Nothing has to be enabled for the free tier to be working, and what it provides is the score plus the benchmark recommendations. Agentless scanning and EASM are the two tempting additions and both need a paid plan — agentless in particular, because "no agent" sounds like "no cost" and means nothing of the kind.

prompt: Which two statements about connecting AWS and GCP accounts to Defender for Cloud are correct? (Choose two.)
choices: The connector uses native cloud identity federation, not stored secrets
Connected accounts receive Secure Score, recommendations and plans
A permanent AWS access key must be pasted into the Azure connector first
Only GCP supports multicloud connection, since AWS is not supported
correctAnswers: The connector uses native cloud identity federation, not stored secrets
Connected accounts receive Secure Score, recommendations and plans
explanation: Federation removes the stored credential, and a connected account is then treated like an Azure one — scored, recommended against, and able to carry Defender plans. The access-key statement is the tempting one because it describes how these integrations used to work, whereas both clouds now connect without a long-lived secret.

prompt: Referring to requirement 1 (a single score summarizing configuration compliance across Azure, AWS, and GCP in one place, prioritized by impact), which Defender for Cloud capability meets this?
choices: Secure Score, aggregated across Azure, AWS and GCP
The regulatory compliance dashboard, scoped to ISO 27001
Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management, on VMs only
Attack path analysis, on the Azure subscription only
correctAnswers: Secure Score, aggregated across Azure, AWS and GCP
explanation: The requirement asks for one impact-prioritized number over all three clouds, which is what Secure Score is. The compliance dashboard is the tempting alternative because it also aggregates posture, whereas it reports control-by-control against one standard rather than producing a single prioritized score.

prompt: Referring to requirement 2 (before onboarding an acquired subsidiary, discover its internet-facing web servers the way an external attacker would), which capability should Relecloud use?
choices: External Attack Surface Management (EASM)
Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management
Agentless virtual machine disk scanning
The regulatory compliance dashboard
correctAnswers: External Attack Surface Management (EASM)
explanation: The phrase "the way an external attacker would" is the whole clue: nothing has been onboarded yet, so any capability that reads your subscriptions has nothing to read. MDVM and agentless scanning are both tempting and both require the asset to be known and connected already, whereas EASM starts from the outside with only a domain name.

prompt: Referring to requirement 3 (scan VMs across the estate for known vulnerabilities and malware without installing any agent), which Defender for Cloud capability applies?
choices: Agentless scanning under Defender CSPM or Defender for Servers
A Conditional Access policy targeting all of the virtual machines
The Content hub in Microsoft Sentinel, for solutions
External Attack Surface Management asset discovery
correctAnswers: Agentless scanning under Defender CSPM or Defender for Servers
explanation: Agentless scanning snapshots the disk and analyses it out of band, which satisfies "without installing any agent" while still finding vulnerabilities and malware. EASM is the tempting neighbour from the previous requirement, whereas it discovers assets from outside and never looks inside a disk.

prompt: Proposed solution: Connect the AWS account and GCP project to Defender for Cloud using their native connectors with CSPM enabled, so Secure Score aggregates configuration compliance across Azure, AWS, and GCP. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: Yes
explanation: The native connectors use identity federation and read each cloud's control plane directly, so one impact-prioritized Secure Score covers all three environments with nothing deployed inside them. Note the prerequisite it still carries: CSPM must be enabled on each connector, since a connector added without it produces an inventory rather than a score.

prompt: Proposed solution: Install the Log Analytics agent on every AWS EC2 instance and GCP VM, then connect the accounts to Defender for Cloud. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: No
explanation: The goal rules out deploying agents first, and this solution begins by deploying one on every instance — so it fails on the stated constraint rather than on capability. It is doubly wrong in practice: the Log Analytics agent is retired, whereas the CSPM connectors were always agentless and would have produced the score on their own.

prompt: Proposed solution: Enable Defender CSPM only on the Azure subscription, and manually track AWS and GCP posture using spreadsheets exported from each cloud console. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: No
explanation: This produces three disconnected views rather than a single automated, impact-prioritized score spanning all three clouds — it does not meet the 'one score' requirement.

prompt: Order the steps to connect an AWS account to Microsoft Defender for Cloud.
reorderItems: Defender for Cloud ▸ Environment settings ▸ Add environment ▸ Amazon Web Services
Name the connector and provide the AWS account ID (single account or management/Organization account)
Select which Defender plans to enable (e.g. CSPM, Servers, Containers, Databases)
Download the CloudFormation template and run it in AWS to create the trusted IAM role
Return to Azure and select Create to finish onboarding
explanation: The connector is created in Azure and named before the template exists, because the template is generated for that specific connector. Running the CloudFormation template before creating the connector is the ordering mistake, and selecting Create in Azure comes last — doing it before the IAM role exists leaves a connector that cannot read anything.

prompt: Build the sequence that adds a regulatory compliance standard to a subscription and produces usable evidence. Not every action in the pool belongs in the answer.
poolItems: Open Defender for Cloud ▸ Regulatory compliance ▸ Manage compliance policies
Choose the scope: a management group or a subscription
Under Security policies, add the standard and assign it
Allow the environment to be evaluated, then review pass/fail evidence per control
Assign the standard at a resource group, to keep its scope narrow
Read the per-control evidence immediately after assigning the standard
Enable every paid Defender plan first, so the standard has data to score
correctOrder: Open Defender for Cloud ▸ Regulatory compliance ▸ Manage compliance policies
Choose the scope: a management group or a subscription
Under Security policies, add the standard and assign it
Allow the environment to be evaluated, then review pass/fail evidence per control
explanation: Scope is chosen before the standard is added, because the same standard behaves differently at a management group than at one subscription — and a resource group is not an available scope at all, which is why that action is excluded rather than merely suboptimal. Reading the evidence immediately is the other excluded action: nothing has been evaluated yet, so the dashboard shows a verdict that is not one.

prompt: Configure this simplified Defender for Cloud environment screen so the subscription gains attack path analysis and the cloud security explorer, while keeping workload-protection cost to a minimum.
explanation: Attack path analysis and the cloud security explorer are unlocked by Defender CSPM, so that toggle alone satisfies the requirement. Defender for Servers is the tempting addition because it also contains posture features, whereas it is a workload-protection plan billed per machine — turning it on would meet the goal and violate the cost constraint attached to it.
